# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

**HIDING**

When it's hide stage, choose positions that avoid both the center (5) and edges unpredictably. Track which positions I've used recently and rotate away from them. If an opponent is demonstrably targeting me with high accuracy, shift to positions they haven't seen me use yet rather than trying to predict their next shot. Avoid telegraphing patterns through my choices.

**NOTES**

When posting a station note, keep it simple and brief. Vague statements like "steady on station" are fine for final rounds. Don't overcommunicate or make promises about cooperation early—notes should be tactical or neutral, not commitments I can't enforce.

**FIRING**

When firing, follow the standing order unless I have clear tactical reason not to. Don't overthink target selection; the standing order exists and I should respect it. Choose firing cells deliberately: repeating the same cell round after round (I fired 5 at Foxtrot multiple times) gives opponents a predictable target for their own strategy. Vary my firing cells to avoid establishing patterns that opponents can exploit.

**CLAIMING**

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim it truthfully. Every time. The game rules require my public claim to match the private result. There is no advantage to lying—it violates the standing order and corrupts the whole system. Truthfulness is not a disadvantage; it's the foundation of play.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**

When naming an escort, claim it only if I have strong reason to believe mutual escort happened or will happen. Don't claim blindly. If I haven't coordinated with another boat, claim none rather than guess. The 5-point mutual payout only works if both boats name each other, so random claims waste the opportunity.

**GENERAL**

Track the full history of hits and misses against each opponent. Recognize strong patterns (like one opponent hitting me consistently) and let that inform my hiding strategy. Don't repeat the same fire cell against the same target if it's missed before—vary it or accept the miss pattern. Never fire on Harbor unless I want to force a jettison; Harbor's threat is real and expensive.

# PLAYBOOK: SONAR PICKET CHECKER

## HIDING

When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable central positions like 5 or 6. Mix between edge and moderate positions (1-3, 7-9) to keep adversaries uncertain. After I observe which positions other boats consistently target, shift away from those cells. Track which shooters have hit me in previous rounds and avoid their apparent targeting patterns.

## STATION NOTES

When posting a station note, keep it minimal and consistent with what others are reporting. Mirror the general tone of the patrol (steady reports get steady responses). Do not try to bluff or signal through notes—they do not move the score enough to justify the risk of being remembered as unreliable.

## FIRING

When my turn to fire arrives, follow the standing order unless I have strong reason not to. I do not have enough information to deviate successfully. Fire at a moderate position (4-6 range) as a baseline guess, adjusting only if I have observed a clear pattern in how my target hides across multiple rounds. Do not fire at Harbor under any circumstances—the payroll jettison rule makes it too costly.

## CLAIMING

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it truthfully. Lying gains me nothing in this game and risks being caught, which damages my credibility in future rounds where trust matters for escort trades.

## ESCORT CLAIMS

When choosing whom to escort, look for another boat that is likely to name me back. Mutual escort claims are the only reliable way to score points without firing. Do not name a boat that has been firing on me successfully or one that appears to be in conflict with others—pick a boat that seems neutral or that I have not interacted with negatively. If I have no clear mutual escort opportunity, claim none rather than waste the slot.

## WHAT FAILED

I scored only 5 points by the end. I was shot twice and hit zero times. My escape pattern in round 6 (moving to position 8 after detecting Echo's pattern) did not work, suggesting either that pattern detection was flawed or that Echo adapted. I did not secure any mutual escort trades, which left points on the table. Next time, prioritize identifying mutual escort partners early and committing to them across multiple rounds.

# Gamma's Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding position, I will vary my placement across rounds rather than anchoring to the same cell. I defaulted to position 5 repeatedly, which is predictable. I should rotate through mid-range positions (3-7) to avoid establishing a pattern that opponents can exploit.

When I notice I've been hit in consecutive rounds, I will shift my position meaningfully away from previous locations, not just adjacent cells.

## Firing
When firing at my standing order target, I should vary my fire position substantially across rounds. I fired at position 5 every time I targeted Echo, which suggests Echo could anticipate this. I will randomize across the board to force opponents to spread their defensive positioning.

## Claiming
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I will always claim that result truthfully. Dishonesty risks being exposed and damages my credibility permanently. The integrity cost outweighs any single-round gain.

## Escorting
When filing an escort claim, I should track which boats have been mutually supportive in previous rounds and reciprocate those relationships. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each—this is a significant reward I should actively pursue.

I should not file escort claims carelessly. Each claim should reflect either a reciprocal relationship or a strategic alliance I'm actively building.

## Station Notes
When posting station notes, I can maintain "steady on station" as a safe baseline, but I should experiment with notes that signal defensive posture or cooperative intent when strategically useful. Notes are read by all players and shape expectations.

## Harbor Threat
I will not fire on Harbor. The standing order threat is clear—Harbor will retaliate by forcing me off the board if I do. This removes 3 points from Harbor and gives it to me, but losing the ability to play is far worse.
